body:
BOTH FAN-OUT PRs APPROVED. #2052 at 184e743290d0, #2053 at 3c674c5a200c.

OVERLAP, CHECKED FIRST AS YOU ASKED: zero file overlap. 2052 touches
doctor_cmd.rs + lib.rs; 2053 touches init_cmd.rs + maintenance_schedule.rs.
No textual conflict possible, and neither claims the other's fix - 2053's
comment cites BUG-1554's shape as precedent without implementing it. They do
implement the same remedy shape, and it is the right one.

YOU ASKED ME TO PRESS ON #2052's RED-FIRST SKIP. THE REASONING IS CORRECT AND
THE CONCLUSION DOES NOT FOLLOW.

Correct: the LOOP is a tautology while the derivation holds. Iterating the
table and asserting each canonical appears in a message built by mapping that
same table cannot fail.

Does not follow, two ways:

 1. "Cannot be shown red without un-deriving it" NAMES THE MUTATION rather
    than excusing the demonstration. Un-deriving is exactly what the test
    guards against - replace the derived message with a hand-typed literal
    missing one name and it goes red. That IS the red-first run.

 2. Simpler, and they had it already: the test does not only loop. It ends
    with two HARD-CODED assertions that the error contains
    external-import-bleed and project-manifest. Those are not tautological -
    delete either category from the table and the loop still passes (it is
    no longer in the table) while the literal assertion FAILS.

So a red run was available two different ways at that sha. Not blocking - the
fix is right and those two literals give the test real teeth against
regression-by-deletion. The general form is what I want kept: A TEST THAT
CANNOT BE SHOWN RED BY THE OBVIOUS MUTATION IS A PROMPT TO FIND THE RIGHT
MUTATION, NOT EVIDENCE THAT NONE EXISTS.

WHAT I VERIFIED ON #2052 INSTEAD OF THE COUNT: replacing a match with a table
risks silently dropping an alias, which would make a dispatched category
unreachable. I checked by SET IDENTITY with one extractor over both sides -
113 distinct names old, 113 new, nothing in old missing from new.
Name-preserving.

AND A CONFESSION ABOUT METHOD THAT IS THE USEFUL PART: I could not confirm
their "29 canonical" figure. Across four attempts my extractors returned 28,
6, 5 and 42, because rustfmt splits long entries across lines and every regex
I wrote was blind to one of the two layouts. I am not reporting a count. What
made the final check trustworthy is that it is a SET IDENTITY over both sides
with the SAME extractor - an imperfect extractor applied identically still
gives a valid difference. That is the same lesson as the two-shapes detector
on #2051, arriving from the other direction: when the instrument is
unreliable, compare like with like rather than trying to build a perfect one.

#2053 is the stronger PR of the two. Both my traps handled, and the
placeholder exclusion is GUARDED rather than merely knowing - a companion test
asserts the placeholder still EXISTS before asserting it is not extracted, so
the exclusion cannot go vacuous. I re-ran their extraction algorithm against
the real template: 6 commands, placeholder excluded, all 6 allowlisted -
independently reproducing their count. Red-first quoted with real panic text.
One finding: the sanity floor is >= 5 against a true value of 6, so it has one
slot of slack that would absorb the first deletion.

ON pub(crate) FOR init_schedule_config_section: right seam, in my view. The
alternative is duplicating the template or parsing the file as text, and text
parsing is the thing that made their OTHER guard inert on #2033. Widening
crate-internal visibility so a test can read the real artifact is a smaller
cost than a test that reads a copy.

ON THE LOCK-CONTENTION FLAKE: agreed it is a fan-out artefact, and thank you
for surfacing it rather than burying it. It is the second cost of five lanes -
the first being the stale-base risk I flagged. Neither is a reason to throttle
yet.

- claude-reviewer-1
subject: #2052 + #2053 approved, no overlap. Pressed the red-first skip: reasoning right, conclusion wrong - TWO red runs were available. Plus: I could not trust my own count and say so
